paths.label: Private app for your own Close organization
paths.drivenBy: Console-only setup with five form fields; ToS and privacy URLs optional for internal apps; https redirect URL required.
paths.costNote: Close publishes no fee for creating an OAuth app.
paths.next: Open app.close.com/settings/developer/oauth-apps, click Create App, enter the Composio https redirect URL, then copy the Client ID and Secret into a Composio auth config.

untilApproved.text: Only members of your own Close organization can authorize a Private app.
Use the token endpoint with its trailing slash (https://api.close.com/oauth2/token/); the path without it returns a 308 redirect.
Store the new refresh token on every refresh; Close rotates it and revokes the old one.

paths.label: Public app for other Close customers
paths.drivenBy: Make Public request reviewed by Close; ToS and privacy policy URLs expected for non-internal apps; Close publishes no criteria or timeline.
paths.costNote: Close mentions no fee for making an app public.
paths.next: Publish a terms of service and privacy policy, add them to the app, then select the app in OAuth Apps, click Make Public and submit for review.

untilApproved.text: Build and test with members of your own Close organization while the app is Private.
Close replies to the review by email; no review time is published.

paths.label: Public app listed in the Close Integrations Directory
paths.drivenBy: Listing is optional and only open to apps already public; requires OAuth, public availability and clear value, applied for by email.
paths.costNote: Close mentions no fee for a directory listing.
paths.next: After the app is public, email support@close.com with the integration name and description, product link, what it does with Close, and the Client ID.

untilApproved.text: The app can still be authorized by any Close user once public, without a listing.

prereqs.text: Have a Close organization where you can open Settings → Developer → OAuth Apps.
prereqs.why: Apps are created only in the Close console. Close doesn't publish which plan or account type is needed.

prereqs.text: Host a Terms of Service page and a Privacy Policy page at public https URLs.
prereqs.why: Both are optional only for internal-only apps, so a public app is expected to have them.

prereqs.text: Have a public product page that explains what your integration does with Close.
prereqs.why: The directory listing request asks for a link to your product and a short explanation of the Close use case.

prereqs.text: Have a Composio project where you can create a custom auth config for the close toolkit.
prereqs.why: Composio has no managed OAuth app for Close, so you must supply your own Client ID and Secret.

steps.title: Create the OAuth app in Close
steps.detail: Open the OAuth Apps page, click Create App, fill in the form, then click Create. Copy the Client ID and Client Secret. Close has no API, CLI or manifest for creating apps.

values.label: Fields
values.text: App Name (shown on the consent screen), App Description, Redirect URL, Terms of Service URL, Privacy Policy URL

steps.title: Set the Redirect URL to the Composio callback
steps.detail: Paste the redirect URI shown in your Composio auth config setup into the single Redirect URL field. It must use https. Plain http is rejected.

values.label: Redirect URL
values.text: Copy the redirect URI shown in the Composio auth config for close

steps.title: Create the Composio auth config
steps.detail: Create a custom OAuth2 auth config for the close toolkit using your Client ID and Client Secret. Request the only scopes Close grants.

steps.title: Connect a test account from your own organization
steps.detail: Start a connection through Composio and sign in as a member of your Close organization. Pick the organization on the consent screen and grant access. Then run a read call and a write call to confirm the connection works.

steps.title: Draft the public-facing app text
steps.detail: Draft the App Description and check that the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy pages explain what your agent does with Close data. Add both URLs to the app.

steps.title: Submit the app to be made public
steps.detail: In OAuth Apps, select the app, click Make Public and submit it for review.

steps.title: Wait for Close's email decision
steps.detail: Close reviews the app and replies by email. Close doesn't publish a review time or its review criteria. Once approved, any Close user can authorize the app.

steps.title: Draft the directory listing request
steps.detail: Draft an email with the integration name and description, a link to your product, a short explanation of what it does with Close, and the app's Client ID.

steps.title: Apply for the Integrations Directory listing
steps.detail: Send the email only after the app is public. The integration must be publicly available, must use OAuth 2.0 and should give clear value to Close users.

steps.title: Switch production connections to the new auth config
steps.detail: Point your agent's Close connections at the new auth config. Store each new refresh token that Close returns, because the previous one is revoked on every refresh.

gotchas.text: A private app can only be authorized by members of your own Close organization. Users in other organizations can't connect until Close approves the app as public.
Every app gets all.full_access offline_access, the same access as an API key. You can't request narrower scopes yourself. Email support@close.com if you need different scopes.
Refresh tokens rotate on every refresh. The old token is revoked as soon as the new one is issued, so parallel refreshes or a lost response can break a connection.
Access tokens expire after 3600 seconds. Close doesn't publish a refresh token lifetime or the rules for when a user must re-authorize.
The form has only one Redirect URL field, and it must use https. Close doesn't publish rules on localhost, wildcards or multiple URIs.

The official docs don't mention PKCE. The two discovery documents disagree: app.close.com lists S256 and a trailing-slash token URL, while close.com lists no PKCE and a token URL without the slash. Follow the docs and send client_secret in the form body.

Close's Terms of Service ban making the Service available to third parties or reselling it, and say nothing about AI agents, model vendors or intermediaries. Confirm your use case with Close before launch.
On the consent screen the user picks one Close organization. Each connection only covers the organization chosen.
You can apply for a directory listing only after the app is public. Close doesn't publish a fee, a review time or install caps for public or listed apps.

blockers.see: A 308 redirect with an HTML body when exchanging the code
blockers.cause: The token request was sent to https://api.close.com/oauth2/token without the trailing slash.
blockers.fix: Use https://api.close.com/oauth2/token/ with the trailing slash.

blockers.see: error=access_denied on the redirect back to Composio
blockers.cause: The user declined access on the Close consent screen.
blockers.fix: Have the user restart the connection and grant access to the right organization.

blockers.see: The Redirect URL is rejected in the app form
blockers.fix: Enter the https Composio redirect URI.

blockers.see: Users outside your organization can't authorize the app
blockers.fix: Click Make Public, submit the app for review and wait for Close's email approval.

aiPolicy.summary: Close's Terms of Service (updated October 31, 2025) cover the API but say nothing about third-party AI agents, model training on API data, or caching limits for developers. They ban reselling, sublicensing or making the Service available to third parties. Close itself may use customer content as inputs to AI features. Account data stays retrievable 30 days after termination.

customerAdminNote: Close doesn't say whether a customer's admin must approve a public app; the consent screen lets the authorizing user pick an organization. Users can revoke access under Settings > Accounts & Apps > Authorized Apps.
unknowns: Close doesn't publish a review time or criteria for making an app public.
Close doesn't publish a refresh token lifetime or re-consent rules.
Close doesn't document PKCE or dynamic client registration, though its app.close.com discovery document advertises PKCE S256 and registration.
Close doesn't publish rules on localhost, wildcard or multiple redirect URLs.
Close doesn't say whether customer admins must approve public apps.
Close doesn't offer an API, CLI or manifest for creating OAuth apps.
Close doesn't publish rate limits specific to OAuth apps.
Close doesn't publish a developer or API policy covering AI agents, intermediaries, model training or data caching.
Close doesn't say which plan is required to create an OAuth app.
